Photograph: Haiyun Jiang/AFP/Getty Images Opinion Nato Never mind Trump – if Europe wants to save Nato, it must win over the American people Leslie Vinjamuri Mark Rutte has the right idea – go beyond Washington and make the case for the transatlantic alliance to the public. They may well have a willing ear Tue 22 Sep 2026 10.30 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.03 EDT Share A t a moment when Europe is focused on persuading Donald Trump to remain committed to Nato, it needs to convince Americans, too. So the presence this evening of the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte , in front of a public audience in Des Moines, Iowa, is significant. This is the home town of Trump’s ambassador to Nato, Matthew Whitaker, and the visit brings the debate over Nato’s future directly to a midwestern audience in a red state that operates far from elite foreign-policy circles in Washington. Rutte’s appearance is long overdue. Russia’s war in Ukraine and uncertainty over the US commitment to European security have forced European leaders to confront their dependence on Washington . While some are pressing for building European capabilities as a means to separate from the US, others see greater European defence spending as essential to keeping the US engaged. Either way, European governments can’t rely solely on meetings with Trump to secure the alliance’s future. Instead, Europe’s leaders need to look beyond Washington and take a tip from Rutte. Making the public case for Nato, the transatlantic partnership, and shared security across the middle of the country, is essential, not optional. This case should begin with the American people. For decades, Americans have supported the transatlantic relationship because they understood that Europe’s security is closely connected to their own. Nato and the transatlantic partnership were part of a wider ambition, designed to make the world safe for democracy, not least for the growth and prosperity this created. Public support has been essential to this undertaking. For many Americans, democracy is now failing to deliver on the promise of prosperity, and in some key areas the contrast with Europe is stark. In the Commonwealth Fund’s 2023 survey , 46% of US adults with lower or average incomes reported skipping or delaying needed healthcare because of cost, compared with 16% in each of the UK, France, Germany and the Netherlands. Populists have been quick to highlight the shortcomings of America’s democracy, and this message has resonated across swaths of the population, particularly rural voters and Americans without a university degree – both central to Trump’s electoral coalition. When it comes to the American public, there is plenty of room for optimism, but in a political context that is ripe for populists to cultivate antagonism toward spending on foreign causes, there is little room for complacency. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs’ polling consistently shows that Americans support Nato and the transatlantic partnership. Its recent survey with Ipsos found that 68% of Americans supported maintaining or increasing the US commitment to Nato. Yet only 47% were confident that European allies would come to America’s defence if it were attacked, down from 62% in 2025. Public support for Ukraine has also remained substantial, even as Americans debate the scale and duration of US assistance; a 2024 survey found that 58% supported sending additional arms and military supplies to Ukraine, and the same number supported economic assistance. European leaders would be wise to invest in a public diplomacy strategy in order to cultivate understanding among Americans outside Washington’s foreign-policy establishment. The secretary general’s decision to travel to Iowa should be seen as a crucial part of Europe’s midwest strategy. Other leading foreign policy organisations have sought to do the same. Over the summer, the Ditchley Foundation used the occasion of America’s 250th to deepen its partnerships across the US, convening roundtables in South Carolina and Illinois. This outreach is essential to counter the persistent myth that Europeans are free-riding on America’s coattails. Europe’s renewed commitment to defence is significant, with a 20% increase in 2025 compared with 2024 among the EU’s 27 member states. This remains poorly understood in the US. Nato’s Annual 2025 report notes that all of Nato’s 32 members met or exceeded the 2% of GDP expenditure target for that year. Allies have committed to investing 5% of GDP annually by 2035 in defence and related security. The precise figures matter, but so does the broader message: that Europe is investing in the capacity to defend itself and contribute to shared security. It would also be smart to highlight the opportunities created by this investment for American companies. Defence cooperation supports jobs and growth opportunities. It also boosts transatlantic supply chains and research partnerships. But the ties that bind Europe and America reach deeper than military procurement. The case for the alliance should ultimately be made in terms that people recognise in their own lives: the security of their jobs, the price and availability of energy, the resilience of the technology they rely on and, above all, the prospect of their families living without the threat of a wider war. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion The transatlantic partnership cannot be secured through presidential diplomacy alone. European leaders should continue engaging the White House, but they must also make their case to the American public. The long-term future of Nato will depend not only on what presidents decide, but on whether citizens on both sides of the Atlantic continue to see the alliance as essential to their security, democracy and prosperity. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/25/four.text: Seventeen military personnel were swept into the Caspian Sea during a training exercise by Kazakhstan’s Naval Forces. Fourteen of them have died and three were rescued.The incident occurred on 24 September in Kazakhstan's Mangystau region. The servicemen who died were born between 2005 and 2007.According to the Kazakh Defence Ministry, the soldiers were disembarking from the Kaisar military vessel in water one metre deep when they were swept into the open sea by strong winds and a sudden deterioration in weather conditions.Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev declared 25 September the day of mourning and expressed his condolences to the families of those who died. He also ordered the authorities to establish the circumstances of the incident.The tragedy has also brought attention to a previous fatal incident during military exercises in the Caspian Sea. In 2015, four servicemen died during military exercises near Aktau after strong winds and waves flooded four armoured personnel carriers.Investigation underwayA government commission headed by Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev has been working at the scene.The Prosecutor General’s Office says investigators have inspected the scene, questioned more than 30 military personnel and seized documents and video footage.According to the preliminary findings, the suspected officials failed to take the necessary measures to ensure the safety of personnel as weather conditions deteriorated.

Zak Ali is the founder of Creative Advisor , an AI-native PR agency helping you turn expertise into a personal brand. getty ​​Before I was old enough to drive, I already knew I could “save 15% or more by switching to Geico,” and that “it’s so easy, a caveman could do it.” I can’t recite my family’s phone numbers, but “800-588-2300, Empire” is so ingrained in my memory that it’ll occasionally show up as a vocal stim. Those lines are stuck in my head because those companies spent decades and millions of dollars putting them there. TV spots only worked if we remembered them, so brands built ads to stick, using mascots, jingles and slogans repeated for years until they felt like part of the household. That’s also why we trusted them. Everyone knew TV ads were expensive, so a brand on TV was a brand that could afford to be there, and it could only keep paying if people kept buying. And when you bought from them, you weren’t buying this random thing you saw on the internet. You were buying from a name brand. Now, when a new product shows up in my feed, my first instinct is to check whether the same thing is on Alibaba. Is this a company with real expertise and a reason to exist, or a marketing operation that knows how to package a commodity for a triple-digit markup? Software raises the same question. Is this tool worth another subscription, or am I paying for a few basic prompts wrapped in a pretty user interface? According to Edelman’s 2026 research on brand growth , 88% of the consumers surveyed said trusting a brand is an important reason to buy from it, about the same as quality and value. But the signals people once used to decide which companies to trust have stopped working, and anyone launching a brand today needs to understand why. ​Anyone Can Look Like A Brand Now ​The trust we gave TV brands hinged on advertising being hard to do. Then the barriers came down. Over the last decade, three changes made it easy for almost anyone to look like a serious company: 1. Distribution: The commercial break isn’t much of a thing anymore. Most viewers cut the cord for ad-free streaming, and started spending more of their free time on social media. There, targeting lets any brand reach likely buyers for a fraction of what a national spot once cost. It doesn’t matter if a company is worth billions of dollars and has been around for 50 years or just started last month, the user sees their ads just the same. 2. Production: Dropshipping lets anyone tap into overseas warehouses and sell a product they’ve never made or touched. AI coding tools let anyone ship software without needing to understand what’s going on under the hood. That’s mostly a good thing, since lower barriers produce businesses that otherwise wouldn’t exist. But owning a business no longer implies that the people behind it have expertise in the thing they’re selling. 3. Polish: AI can now generate convincing ads, product photos, emails and videos. So a slick website or a professional-looking ad doesn’t tell you much about the culture, standards or values of the company behind it anymore. Ironically, some of that polish may actually be a distrust signal. A recent Gartner survey found that 57% of consumers say AI-generated content has made them less trusting of brand messaging. So when anyone can reach you, anyone can own a product and anyone can look legitimate, what are the new trust signals? ​Why The People Behind The Brand Matter ​Commercial advertising worked as a trust signal because it put the brand’s reputation on the line. A company that told the whole country its product was great had a lot to lose if it wasn’t. A visible founder or team works the same way. A dropshipper can abandon a brand name overnight and relaunch under a new one. But a person can’t abandon their face. When someone puts their name, expertise and track record behind a product, they give customers something to hold them accountable to. That accountability is what puts customers at ease. Everyone understands self-preservation, so when a company or a person is willing to risk their reputation on a product, it makes them more trustworthy. We don’t need to trust their intentions, only their self-interest. A faceless brand with no individual points of accountability outside of a support email doesn’t have that same incentive to deliver for its customers. Does this mean giant faceless brands are going to start failing? No. They already spent decades building trust they can keep drawing on. Their names themselves are a trust signal. And trying to force their CEOs to become influencers could actually do more harm to their brands than good. What’s ending is the ability to start a brand that way. A new company can’t just buy the trust incumbents built by being the soundtrack to your living room over years. It has to earn it through people. ​How To Build A Brand With A Face ​There is no one right way to build a face for your brand. For a B2B SaaS company, it may mean cultivating an audience by posting on LinkedIn. For a luxury e-commerce business, it may mean going to trade shows and meeting with tastemakers in their industry. The tactics that are right for one industry may be totally different for yours. At the end of the day, what matters is showing up authentically in front of the people that you want as customers or advocates in your space. Once you discover where your people are, demonstrate why you’re an authority in your space by talking about your industry freely. Share your origin story, your wins and your setbacks. Build community by reaching out to others and engaging with the people who reach out to you. Finally, find ways to add as much value as you can, as often as you can. As the cost of looking like a brand approaches zero, the people behind your brand are what give you your edge.​ Forbes Business Development Council is an invitation-only community for sales and biz dev executives. https://hvg.hu/360/20261112_kulturalis-a.text: Joan Wasser, művésznevén Joan as Police Woman november 18-án lép fel a Magyar Zene Házában. A New York-i dalszerző-énekessel a versek erejéről és a névadó zsarusorozatról is beszélgettünk. Az Interview magazinban David Byrne-nel beszélgetett nemrég, egyebek mellett a New York-i biciklizés örömeiről. Bringázás közben írt dalt? Egyet. A Damn Devotion albumomon lévő Valid Jagger így született. Igazi forróság volt aznap, úgy 38 fok. Egy barátomat látogattam meg, és miközben a háza felé bicikliztem, befészkelte magát a fejembe egy dallam. Nem hagyott nyugodni, úgyhogy amikor megérkeztem, nem szálltam le, hanem körözni kezdtem szép lassan a háztömb körül, jó fél órán át a tikkasztó hőségben. A dallamhoz közben szavak is társultak. Meditatív állapot volt, a bicajozás és a dalszerzés képes erre. New Yorknak melyik részén történt mindez? New Yorkban a metró a fő tömegközlekedési eszköz. A metrózás is kedvez a dalszerzésnek? A metró nem annyira a dalszerzés, mint inkább az emberiség tanulmányozásának helyszíne. A New York-i életet a metrón lehet a maga rendkívül sokszínűségében megfigyelni. És ezek a metrós megfigyelések nemritkán szavakká alakulnak. Miközben olvastam a David Byrne-nel folytatott beszélgetést, úgy tűnt, hol ő az interjúvoló, hol meg ön. Nem került szóba az együttműködés lehetősége? Mégiscsak két zenész beszélgetett. A NAV és az ügyészség nyomozói csütörtök reggel jelentek meg a lakiteleki Népfőiskola Alapítványnál.
